addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

Use when invoking models, setting up Knowledge Bases, creating agents, applying guardrails, deploying to AgentCore, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing models (Claude, Llama, [infra], Titan). Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. content.content:
1	---
2	redu_schema: 2
3	repo: https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui
4	plan:
5	  tool: deploy_compose
6	  image: ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main
7	  port: 8080
8	  vm: m1.medium
9	  flavor_id: "3"
10	  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
11	  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
12	bootstrap:
13	  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
14	  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
15	  source: open-webui
16	quirks:
17	  - "DO NOT BUILD FROM SOURCE. Open WebUI publishes ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui and the repo is large. Pin a release tag rather than :main once you know which one you ran, so a redeploy cannot silently move the app under the user."
18	  - "⛔ DELETE THE OLLAMA SERVICE FROM THEIR COMPOSE. The compose in their repo bundles ollama/ollama alongside the app, and copying it verbatim onto a redu VM is the single most expensive mistake available here: there is no GPU, the image is gigabytes, and models are gigabytes more, so it will fill the disk and then run inference on the CPU at unusable speed. Deploy the app service ALONE and point it at a model provider over the network. That is one service, not two."
19	  - "MODEL PROVIDER: with Ollama gone the app has no models until it is given one. Either set OPENAI_API_KEY (plus OPENAI_API_BASE_URL if it is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint rather than OpenAI itself), or set OLLAMA_BASE_URL to an Ollama the user already runs somewhere reachable. Ask the user which; do NOT put a key in the compose file you commit, pass it as env at deploy time. A deploy with no provider comes up healthy and shows an empty model list, which reads like a broken deploy and is not one."
20	  - "⛔ SET WEBUI_SECRET_KEY EXPLICITLY. It signs the session JWTs, and env.py checks it at startup and states outright that it is a hard requirement when authentication is enabled. Generate one long random value, pass it as env, and pass the SAME one on every redeploy: change it and every signed-in user is logged out, and anything encrypted with it (OAuth client info and session tokens both default to deriving from it) stops decrypting."
21	  - "DATABASE: set DATABASE_URL to the managed Postgres. deploy_compose with database:'managed' APPENDS DATABASE_URL to the project .env already, and env.py rewrites a postgres:// prefix to postgresql:// on its own, so this wiring is genuinely one line. Your compose still has to reference it explicitly (DATABASE_URL: \"\${DATABASE_URL}\") because deploy_compose writes the .env and never edits your compose. WITHOUT it the app silently uses sqlite:///{DATA_DIR}/webui.db inside the container: every chat, user and setting disappears on the next redeploy with no error."
22	  - "⛔ CLAIM THE ADMIN ACCOUNT IMMEDIATELY. A fresh instance has no users and the FIRST account to sign up becomes the administrator. The source is explicit that this first-admin path is deliberately not gated by the signup toggle, so turning signups off later does not close the window; it is open from the moment the URL resolves. Claim it the second the deploy reports ready, then turn signups off from the admin panel if the user wants a private instance."
23	  - "PORT 8080 INSIDE THE CONTAINER. Their own compose maps host 3000 to container 8080, which is exactly the confusion to avoid here: pass 8080 to deploy_compose, because that is the port the app actually listens on."
24	  - "PERSIST /app/backend/data. Even with Postgres holding users and chats, that directory carries uploaded files, RAG document storage and the vector index. A named volume on it is not optional if the user will upload anything."
25	  - "RAM IS THE REAL SIZING CONSTRAINT, NOT CPU. The RAG pipeline loads a sentence-transformers embedding model into the app process on first use, so idle memory and working memory are very different numbers. m1.medium (4 GB) is the floor for chat-only use. If the user will embed documents, plan m1.large and say so before deploying rather than discovering it as an OOM kill afterwards."
26	  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr; fits the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the DB VM to the app flavor and doubles the bill), port 8080."
27	  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source, so there is no repo to point deploy_compose at. Write a one-service docker-compose.yml locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo."
28	  - "FIRST BOOT IS SLOW. The image is large and the app runs its migrations against the fresh Postgres before it serves. Give the health check room; a probe that gives up early looks like a failed deploy on a container that is still starting normally."
29	  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. redu.md is committed and read by the next person. The admin account, the WEBUI_SECRET_KEY and any model-provider API key belong to the user. Hand them over in the session; the deploy log records that the account was claimed, never what with."
30	  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back, adding anything you hit that is not already here. The next person's deploy starts from yours."
31	  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but keeps the managed Postgres so chat history is not lost by accident, and that DB keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. To stop paying entirely the user must also delete_database."
32	---
33	
34	# Self-host Open WebUI on redu
35	
36	A private ChatGPT-style interface over whichever models you choose: one container, a managed
37	Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS URL. Your conversations stay in your own database, in the EU.
38	
39	## What this deploys
40	
41	- **Open WebUI** from the official image, on one m1.medium VM, container port 8080.
42	- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so users and chat history survive every redeploy.
43	- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.
44	
45	About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.
46	
47	It does not include a model. Point it at OpenAI, at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or at an
48	Ollama you already run.
49	
50	## Deploy
51	
52	Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
53	directory containing this file:
54	
55	    Read redu.md and deploy Open WebUI on redu.
56	
57	The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.
58	
59	## The three that actually break it
60	
61	**The bundled Ollama.** Open WebUI's own compose ships an `ollama` service next to the app.
62	Copying it onto a VM with no GPU downloads gigabytes, fills the disk and then runs inference on
63	the CPU. Deploy the app on its own.
64	
65	**The database.** Without `DATABASE_URL` the app uses SQLite inside the container, and every
66	chat vanishes on the next redeploy. It does not warn you.
67	
68	**The secret key.** Set `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` yourself and keep it. Change it and everyone is
69	logged out and anything derived from it stops decrypting.
70	
71	## Claiming the admin account
72	
73	The first account to sign up becomes the administrator, and that is true from the moment the URL
74	resolves. Run this as soon as the deploy reports ready.
75	
76	```bash
77	#!/usr/bin/env bash
78	# Claim the Open WebUI admin account, and PROVE it took.
79	#   ./claim-admin.sh openwebui-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud you@example.com
80	set -eu
81	HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"
82	EMAIL="${2:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"
83	
84	TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
85	
86	# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
87	PASS="[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"
88	
89	# Body on stdin, never in argv: an argument would show up in ps for every user on the machine.
90	post() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "https://$HOST$1" \
91	           -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-; }
92	
93	code=$(printf '{"name":"Admin","email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" \
94	  | post /api/v1/auths/signup)
95	if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
96	  echo "signup failed: HTTP $code" >&2
97	  echo "if this says the instance already has users, someone else claimed it. Delete and redeploy." >&2
98	  cat "$TMP/body" >&2
99	  exit 1
100	fi
101	
102	# A 200 on signup does NOT prove the account can sign in again. This is the actual proof.
103	code=$(printf '{"email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" | post /api/v1/auths/signin)
104	[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the account exists but it does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }
105	
106	# The first account is meant to be the administrator. Confirm it, do not assume it.
107	grep -q '"role":"admin"' "$TMP/body" \
108	  || { echo "signed in, but this account is not an admin. Someone claimed it first." >&2; exit 1; }
109	
110	cat <<EOF
111	
112	Admin account claimed, and the sign-in was verified.
113	  URL:      https://$HOST
114	  Email:    $EMAIL
115	  Password: [REDACTED:value]
116	
117	Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
118	Next: turn signups off in the admin panel if this is meant to be private.
119	EOF
120	```
121	
122	It prints the credentials once. They do not go in this file.
123	
124	## Deploy log
125	
126	- Not yet deployed. The first real run replaces this line with its measured time, flavor and
127	  hourly rate, and corrects anything above that turned out to be wrong.

# Self-host Open WebUI on redu

A private ChatGPT-style interface over whichever models you choose: one container, a managed
Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS URL. Your conversations stay in your own database, in the EU.

## What this deploys

- **Open WebUI** from the official image, on one m1.medium VM, container port 8080.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so users and chat history survive every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

It does not include a model. Point it at OpenAI, at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or at an
Ollama you already run.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Open WebUI on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The three that actually break it

**The bundled Ollama.** Open WebUI's own compose ships an `ollama` service next to the app.
Copying it onto a VM with no GPU downloads gigabytes, fills the disk and then runs inference on
the CPU. Deploy the app on its own.

**The database.** Without `DATABASE_URL` the app uses SQLite inside the container, and every
chat vanishes on the next redeploy. It does not warn you.

**The secret key.** Set `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` yourself and keep it. Change it and everyone is
logged out and anything derived from it stops decrypting.

## Claiming the admin account

The first account to sign up becomes the administrator, and that is true from the moment the URL
resolves. Run this as soon as the deploy reports ready.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim the Open WebUI admin account, and PROVE it took.
#   ./claim-admin.sh openwebui-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud you@example.com
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"
EMAIL="${2:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
PASS="[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Body on stdin, never in argv: an argument would show up in ps for every user on the machine.
post() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "https://$HOST$1" \
           -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-; }

code=$(printf '{"name":"Admin","email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" \
  | post /api/v1/auths/signup)
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "signup failed: HTTP $code" >&2
  echo "if this says the instance already has users, someone else claimed it. Delete and redeploy." >&2
  cat "$TMP/body" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# A 200 on signup does NOT prove the account can sign in again. This is the actual proof.
code=$(printf '{"email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" | post /api/v1/auths/signin)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the account exists but it does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# The first account is meant to be the administrator. Confirm it, do not assume it.
grep -q '"role":"admin"' "$TMP/body" \
  || { echo "signed in, but this account is not an admin. Someone claimed it first." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account claimed, and the sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Email:    $EMAIL
  Password: [REDACTED:value]

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
Next: turn signups off in the admin panel if this is meant to be private.
EOF
```

It prints the credentials once. They do not go in this file.

# Open WebUI on redu — ONE service, deliberately.
#
# Upstream's compose ships an `ollama` service next to the app. On a GPU-less VM that
# downloads gigabytes, fills the disk, and then runs inference on the CPU. The model
# provider is reached over the network instead, through the env passed at deploy time.
services:
  open-webui:
    image: ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:v0.11.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      # Left side is the HOST port redu proxies; 8080 is what the app listens on inside.
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      # deploy_compose appends these to the project .env; this file has to reference
      # them explicitly, because redu writes the .env and never edits the compose.
      DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL}"
      WEBUI_SECRET_KEY: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      # Model provider — supplied at deploy time, never committed here.
      OPENAI_API_KEY: "«REDACTED:assigned:06d36b98»}"
      OPENAI_API_BASE_URL: "${OPENAI_API_BASE_URL:-}"
      OLLAMA_BASE_URL: "${OLLAMA_BASE_URL:-}"
      ENABLE_OLLAMA_API: "${ENABLE_OLLAMA_API:-false}"
    volumes:
      # Uploads, RAG document storage and the vector index live here, not in Postgres.
      - open-webui-data:/app/backend/data

volumes:

# Self-host Open WebUI on redu

A private ChatGPT-style interface over whichever models you choose: one container, a managed
Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS URL. Your conversations stay in your own database, in the EU.

## What this deploys

- **Open WebUI** from the official image, on one m1.medium VM, container port 8080.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so users and chat history survive every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

It does not include a model. Point it at OpenAI, at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or at an
Ollama you already run.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Open WebUI on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The three that actually break it

**The bundled Ollama.** Open WebUI's own compose ships an `ollama` service next to the app.
Copying it onto a VM with no GPU downloads gigabytes, fills the disk and then runs inference on
the CPU. Deploy the app on its own.

**The database.** Without `DATABASE_URL` the app uses SQLite inside the container, and every
chat vanishes on the next redeploy. It does not warn you.

**The secret key.** Set `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` yourself and keep it. Change it and everyone is
logged out and anything derived from it stops decrypting.

## Claiming the admin account

The first account to sign up becomes the administrator, and that is true from the moment the URL
resolves. Run this as soon as the deploy reports ready.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim the Open WebUI admin account, and PROVE it took.
#   ./claim-admin.sh openwebui-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud you@example.com
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"
EMAIL="${2:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
PASS="[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Body on stdin, never in argv: an argument would show up in ps for every user on the machine.
post() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "https://$HOST$1" \
           -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-; }

code=$(printf '{"name":"Admin","email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" \
  | post /api/v1/auths/signup)
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "signup failed: HTTP $code" >&2
  echo "if this says the instance already has users, someone else claimed it. Delete and redeploy." >&2
  cat "$TMP/body" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# A 200 on signup does NOT prove the account can sign in again. This is the actual proof.
code=$(printf '{"email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" | post /api/v1/auths/signin)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the account exists but it does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# The first account is meant to be the administrator. Confirm it, do not assume it.
grep -q '"role":"admin"' "$TMP/body" \
  || { echo "signed in, but this account is not an admin. Someone claimed it first." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account claimed, and the sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Email:    $EMAIL
  Password: [REDACTED:value]

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
Next: turn signups off in the admin panel if this is meant to be private.
EOF
```

It prints the credentials once. They do not go in this file.

# Open WebUI on redu — ONE service, deliberately.
#
# Upstream's compose ships an `ollama` service next to the app. On a GPU-less VM that
# downloads gigabytes, fills the disk, and then runs inference on the CPU. The model
# provider is reached over the network instead, through the env passed at deploy time.
services:
  open-webui:
    image: ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:v0.11.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      # Left side is the HOST port redu proxies; 8080 is what the app listens on inside.
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      # deploy_compose appends these to the project .env; this file has to reference
      # them explicitly, because redu writes the .env and never edits the compose.
      DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL}"
      WEBUI_SECRET_KEY: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      # Model provider — supplied at deploy time, never committed here.
      OPENAI_API_KEY: "«REDACTED:assigned:06d36b98»}"
      OPENAI_API_BASE_URL: "${OPENAI_API_BASE_URL:-}"
      OLLAMA_BASE_URL: "${OLLAMA_BASE_URL:-}"
      ENABLE_OLLAMA_API: "${ENABLE_OLLAMA_API:-false}"
    volumes:
      # Uploads, RAG document storage and the vector index live here, not in Postgres.
      - open-webui-data:/app/backend/data

volumes:
  open-webui-data:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim the Open WebUI admin account, and PROVE it took.
#   ./claim-admin.sh openwebui-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud you@example.com
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"
EMAIL="${2:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
PASS="[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Body on stdin, never in argv: an argument would show up in ps for every user on the machine.
post() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "https://$HOST$1" \
           -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-; }

code=$(printf '{"name":"Admin","email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" \
  | post /api/v1/auths/signup)
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "signup failed: HTTP $code" >&2
  echo "if this says the instance already has users, someone else claimed it. Delete and redeploy." >&2
  cat "$TMP/body" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# A 200 on signup does NOT prove the account can sign in again. This is the actual proof.
code=$(printf '{"email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" | post /api/v1/auths/signin)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the account exists but it does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# The first account is meant to be the administrator. Confirm it, do not assume it.
grep -q '"role":"admin"' "$TMP/body" \

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim the Open WebUI admin account, and PROVE it took.
#   ./claim-admin.sh openwebui-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud you@example.com
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"
EMAIL="${2:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
PASS="[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Body on stdin, never in argv: an argument would show up in ps for every user on the machine.
post() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "https://$HOST$1" \
           -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-; }

code=$(printf '{"name":"Admin","email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" \
  | post /api/v1/auths/signup)
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "signup failed: HTTP $code" >&2
  echo "if this says the instance already has users, someone else claimed it. Delete and redeploy." >&2
  cat "$TMP/body" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# A 200 on signup does NOT prove the account can sign in again. This is the actual proof.
code=$(printf '{"email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" | post /api/v1/auths/signin)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the account exists but it does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# The first account is meant to be the administrator. Confirm it, do not assume it.
grep -q '"role":"admin"' "$TMP/body" \
  || { echo "signed in, but this account is not an admin. Someone claimed it first." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account claimed, and the sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Email:    $EMAIL
  Password: [REDACTED:value]

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
Next: turn signups off in the admin panel if this is meant to be private.
EOF

# Open WebUI on redu — ONE service, deliberately.
#
# Upstream's compose ships an `ollama` service next to the app. On a GPU-less VM that
# downloads gigabytes, fills the disk, and then runs inference on the CPU. The model
# provider is reached over the network instead, through the env passed at deploy time.
services:
  open-webui:
    image: ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:v0.11.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      # Left side is the HOST port redu proxies; 8080 is what the app listens on inside.
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      # deploy_compose appends these to the project .env; this file has to reference
      # them explicitly, because redu writes the .env and never edits the compose.
      DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL}"
      WEBUI_SECRET_KEY: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      # Pinned up front, so the app's idea of its own URL survives a redeploy.
      WEBUI_URL: "${WEBUI_URL}"
      # Model provider — supplied at deploy time, never committed here.
      OPENAI_API_KEY: "«REDACTED:assigned:06d36b98»}"
      OPENAI_API_BASE_URL: "${OPENAI_API_BASE_URL:-}"
      OLLAMA_BASE_URL: "${OLLAMA_BASE_URL:-}"
      ENABLE_OLLAMA_API: "${ENABLE_OLLAMA_API:-false}"
    volumes:
      # Uploads, RAG document storage and the vector index live here, not in Postgres.
      - open-webui-data:/app/backend/data

volumes:
  open-webui-data:

input.redu_md:
---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main
  port: 8080
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: open-webui
quirks:
  - "DO NOT BUILD FROM SOURCE. Open WebUI publishes ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui and the repo is large. Pin a release tag rather than :main once you know which one you ran, so a redeploy cannot silently move the app under the user."
  - "⛔ DELETE THE OLLAMA SERVICE FROM THEIR COMPOSE. The compose in their repo bundles ollama/ollama alongside the app, and copying it verbatim onto a redu VM is the single most expensive mistake available here: there is no GPU, the image is gigabytes, and models are gigabytes more, so it will fill the disk and then run inference on the CPU at unusable speed. Deploy the app service ALONE and point it at a model provider over the network. That is one service, not two."
  - "MODEL PROVIDER: with Ollama gone the app has no models until it is given one. Either set OPENAI_API_KEY (plus OPENAI_API_BASE_URL if it is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint rather than OpenAI itself), or set OLLAMA_BASE_URL to an Ollama the user already runs somewhere reachable. Ask the user which; do NOT put a key in the compose file you commit, pass it as env at deploy time. A deploy with no provider comes up healthy and shows an empty model list, which reads like a broken deploy and is not one."
  - "⛔ SET WEBUI_SECRET_KEY EXPLICITLY. It signs the session JWTs, and env.py checks it at startup and states outright that it is a hard requirement when authentication is enabled. Generate one long random value, pass it as env, and pass the SAME one on every redeploy: change it and every signed-in user is logged out, and anything encrypted with it (OAuth client info and session tokens both default to deriving from it) stops decrypting."
  - "DATABASE: set DATABASE_URL to the managed Postgres. deploy_compose with database:'managed' APPENDS DATABASE_URL to the project .env already, and env.py rewrites a postgres:// prefix to postgresql:// on its own, so this wiring is genuinely one line. Your compose still has to reference it explicitly (DATABASE_URL: \"\${DATABASE_URL}\") because deploy_compose writes the .env and never edits your compose. WITHOUT it the app silently uses sqlite:///{DATA_DIR}/webui.db inside the container: every chat, user and setting disappears on the next redeploy with no error."
  - "⛔ CLAIM THE ADMIN ACCOUNT IMMEDIATELY. A fresh instance has no users and the FIRST account to sign up becomes the administrator. The source is explicit that this first-admin path is deliberately not gated by the signup toggle, so turning signups off later does not close the window; it is open from the moment the URL resolves. Claim it the second the deploy reports ready, then turn signups off from the admin panel if the user wants a private instance."
  - "PORT 8080 INSIDE THE CONTAINER. Their own compose maps host 3000 to container 8080, which is exactly the confusion to avoid here: pass 8080 to deploy_compose, because that is the port the app actually listens on."
  - "PERSIST /app/backend/data. Even with Postgres holding users and chats, that directory carries uploaded files, RAG document storage and the vector index. A named volume on it is not optional if the user will upload anything."
  - "RAM IS THE REAL SIZING CONSTRAINT, NOT CPU. The RAG pipeline loads a sentence-transformers embedding model into the app process on first use, so idle memory and working memory are very different numbers. m1.medium (4 GB) is the floor for chat-only use. If the user will embed documents, plan m1.large and say so before deploying rather than discovering it as an OOM kill afterwards."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr; fits the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the DB VM to the app flavor and doubles the bill), port 8080."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source, so there is no repo to point deploy_compose at. Write a one-service docker-compose.yml locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo."
  - "FIRST BOOT IS SLOW. The image is large and the app runs its migrations against the fresh Postgres before it serves. Give the health check room; a probe that gives up early looks like a failed deploy on a container that is still starting normally."
  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. redu.md is committed and read by the next person. The admin account, the WEBUI_SECRET_KEY and any model-provider API key belong to the user. Hand them over in the session; the deploy log records that the account was claimed, never what with."
  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back, adding anything you hit that is not already here. The next person's deploy starts from yours."
  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but keeps the managed Postgres so chat history is not lost by accident, and that DB keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. To stop paying entirely the user must also delete_database."

# Self-host Open WebUI on redu

A private ChatGPT-style interface over whichever models you choose: one container, a managed
Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS URL. Your conversations stay in your own database, in the EU.

## What this deploys

- **Open WebUI** from the official image, on one m1.medium VM, container port 8080.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so users and chat history survive every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

It does not include a model. Point it at OpenAI, at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or at an
Ollama you already run.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Open WebUI on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The three that actually break it

**The bundled Ollama.** Open WebUI's own compose ships an `ollama` service next to the app.
Copying it onto a VM with no GPU downloads gigabytes, fills the disk and then runs inference on
the CPU. Deploy the app on its own.

**The database.** Without `DATABASE_URL` the app uses SQLite inside the container, and every
chat vanishes on the next redeploy. It does not warn you.

**The secret key.** Set `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` yourself and keep it. Change it and everyone is
logged out and anything derived from it stops decrypting.

## Claiming the admin account

The first account to sign up becomes the administrator, and that is true from the moment the URL
resolves. Run this as soon as the deploy reports ready.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim the Open WebUI admin account, and PROVE it took.
#   ./claim-admin.sh openwebui-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud you@example.com
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"
EMAIL="${2:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
PASS="[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Body on stdin, never in argv: an argument would show up in ps for every user on the machine.
post() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "https://$HOST$1" \
           -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-; }

code=$(printf '{"name":"Admin","email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" \
  | post /api/v1/auths/signup)
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "signup failed: HTTP $code" >&2
  echo "if this says the instance already has users, someone else claimed it. Delete and redeploy." >&2
  cat "$TMP/body" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# A 200 on signup does NOT prove the account can sign in again. This is the actual proof.
code=$(printf '{"email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" | post /api/v1/auths/signin)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the account exists but it does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# The first account is meant to be the administrator. Confirm it, do not assume it.
grep -q '"role":"admin"' "$TMP/body" \
  || { echo "signed in, but this account is not an admin. Someone claimed it first." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account claimed, and the sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Email:    $EMAIL
  Password: [REDACTED:value]

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
Next: turn signups off in the admin panel if this is meant to be private.
EOF
```

It prints the credentials once. They do not go in this file.

---
last_deploy:
  id: 420
  date: 2026-08-16
  status: ready
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main
  port: 8080
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: open-webui
quirks:
  - "DO NOT BUILD FROM SOURCE. Open WebUI publishes ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui and the repo is large. Pin a release tag rather than :main once you know which one you ran, so a redeploy cannot silently move the app under the user."
  - "⛔ DELETE THE OLLAMA SERVICE FROM THEIR COMPOSE. The compose in their repo bundles ollama/ollama alongside the app, and copying it verbatim onto a redu VM is the single most expensive mistake available here: there is no GPU, the image is gigabytes, and models are gigabytes more, so it will fill the disk and then run inference on the CPU at unusable speed. Deploy the app service ALONE and point it at a model provider over the network. That is one service, not two."
  - "MODEL PROVIDER: with Ollama gone the app has no models until it is given one. Either set OPENAI_API_KEY (plus OPENAI_API_BASE_URL if it is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint rather than OpenAI itself), or set OLLAMA_BASE_URL to an Ollama the user already runs somewhere reachable. Ask the user which; do NOT put a key in the compose file you commit, pass it as env at deploy time. A deploy with no provider comes up healthy and shows an empty model list, which reads like a broken deploy and is not one."
  - "⛔ SET WEBUI_SECRET_KEY EXPLICITLY. It signs the session JWTs, and env.py checks it at startup and states outright that it is a hard requirement when authentication is enabled. Generate one long random value, pass it as env, and pass the SAME one on every redeploy: change it and every signed-in user is logged out, and anything encrypted with it (OAuth client info and session tokens both default to deriving from it) stops decrypting."
  - "DATABASE: set DATABASE_URL to the managed Postgres. deploy_compose with database:'managed' APPENDS DATABASE_URL to the project .env already, and env.py rewrites a postgres:// prefix to postgresql:// on its own, so this wiring is genuinely one line. Your compose still has to reference it explicitly (DATABASE_URL: \"\${DATABASE_URL}\") because deploy_compose writes the .env and never edits your compose. WITHOUT it the app silently uses sqlite:///{DATA_DIR}/webui.db inside the container: every chat, user and setting disappears on the next redeploy with no error."
  - "⛔ CLAIM THE ADMIN ACCOUNT IMMEDIATELY. A fresh instance has no users and the FIRST account to sign up becomes the administrator. The source is explicit that this first-admin path is deliberately not gated by the signup toggle, so turning signups off later does not close the window; it is open from the moment the URL resolves. Claim it the second the deploy reports ready, then turn signups off from the admin panel if the user wants a private instance."
  - "PORT 8080 INSIDE THE CONTAINER. Their own compose maps host 3000 to container 8080, which is exactly the confusion to avoid here: pass 8080 to deploy_compose, because that is the port the app actually listens on."
  - "PERSIST /app/backend/data. Even with Postgres holding users and chats, that directory carries uploaded files, RAG document storage and the vector index. A named volume on it is not optional if the user will upload anything."
  - "RAM IS THE REAL SIZING CONSTRAINT, NOT CPU. The RAG pipeline loads a sentence-transformers embedding model into the app process on first use, so idle memory and working memory are very different numbers. m1.medium (4 GB) is the floor for chat-only use. If the user will embed documents, plan m1.large and say so before deploying rather than discovering it as an OOM kill afterwards."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr; fits the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the DB VM to the app flavor and doubles the bill), port 8080."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source, so there is no repo to point deploy_compose at. Write a one-service docker-compose.yml locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo."
  - "FIRST BOOT IS SLOW. The image is large and the app runs its migrations against the fresh Postgres before it serves. Give the health check room; a probe that gives up early looks like a failed deploy on a container that is still starting normally."
  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. redu.md is committed and read by the next person. The admin account, the WEBUI_SECRET_KEY and any model-provider API key belong to the user. Hand them over in the session; the deploy log records that the account was claimed, never what with."
  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back, adding anything you hit that is not already here. The next person's deploy starts from yours."
  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but keeps the managed Postgres so chat history is not lost by accident, and that DB keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. To stop paying entirely the user must also delete_database."

# Self-host Open WebUI on redu

A private ChatGPT-style interface over whichever models you choose: one container, a managed
Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS URL. Your conversations stay in your own database, in the EU.

## What this deploys

- **Open WebUI** from the official image, on one m1.medium VM, container port 8080.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so users and chat history survive every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

It does not include a model. Point it at OpenAI, at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or at an
Ollama you already run.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Open WebUI on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The three that actually break it

**The bundled Ollama.** Open WebUI's own compose ships an `ollama` service next to the app.
Copying it onto a VM with no GPU downloads gigabytes, fills the disk and then runs inference on
the CPU. Deploy the app on its own.

**The database.** Without `DATABASE_URL` the app uses SQLite inside the container, and every
chat vanishes on the next redeploy. It does not warn you.

**The secret key.** Set `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` yourself and keep it. Change it and everyone is
logged out and anything derived from it stops decrypting.

## Claiming the admin account

The first account to sign up becomes the administrator, and that is true from the moment the URL
resolves. Run this as soon as the deploy reports ready.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim the Open WebUI admin account, and PROVE it took.
#   ./claim-admin.sh openwebui-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud you@example.com
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"
EMAIL="${2:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
PASS="[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Body on stdin, never in argv: an argument would show up in ps for every user on the machine.
post() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "https://$HOST$1" \
           -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-; }

code=$(printf '{"name":"Admin","email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" \
  | post /api/v1/auths/signup)
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "signup failed: HTTP $code" >&2
  echo "if this says the instance already has users, someone else claimed it. Delete and redeploy." >&2
  cat "$TMP/body" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# A 200 on signup does NOT prove the account can sign in again. This is the actual proof.
code=$(printf '{"email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" | post /api/v1/auths/signin)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the account exists but it does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# The first account is meant to be the administrator. Confirm it, do not assume it.
grep -q '"role":"admin"' "$TMP/body" \
  || { echo "signed in, but this account is not an admin. Someone claimed it first." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account claimed, and the sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Email:    $EMAIL
  Password: [REDACTED:value]

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
Next: turn signups off in the admin panel if this is meant to be private.
EOF
```

It prints the credentials once. They do not go in this file.

Your conversations stay in your own database, in the EU. ## What this deploys - **Open WebUI** from the official image, on one m1.medium VM, container port 8080. - **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so users and chat history survive every redeploy. - A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS. About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time. It does not include a model. Point it at OpenAI, at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or at an Ollama you already run. ## Deploy Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a directory containing this file: Read redu.md and deploy Open WebUI on redu. The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything. ## The three that actually break it **The bundled Ollama.** Open WebUI's own compose ships an `ollama` service next to the app. Copying it onto a VM with no GPU downloads gigabytes, fills the disk and then runs inference on the CPU. Deploy the app on its own. **The database.** Without `DATABASE_URL` the app uses SQLite inside the container, and every chat vanishes on the next redeploy. It does not warn you. **The secret key.** Set `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` yourself and keep it. Change it and everyone is logged out and anything derived from it stops decrypting. ## Claiming the admin account The first account to sign up becomes the administrator, and that is true from the moment the URL resolves. Run this as soon as the deploy reports ready. ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # Claim the Open WebUI admin account, and PROVE it took. # ./claim-admin.sh openwebui-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud you@example.com set -eu HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh }" EMAIL="${2:?usage: claim-admin.sh }" TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT # Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell. PASS="A7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)" # Body on stdin, never in argv: an argument would show up in ps for every user on the machine. post() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "https://$HOST$1" \ -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-; } code=$(printf '{"name":"Admin","email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" \ | post /api/v1/auths/signup) if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then echo "signup failed: HTTP $code" >&2 echo "if this says the instance already has users, someone else claimed it. Delete and redeploy." >&2 cat "$TMP/body" >&2 exit 1 fi # A 200 on signup does NOT prove the account can sign in again. directory containing this file:

EMAIL="${2:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

PASS="[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Self-host Open WebUI on redu

A private ChatGPT-style interface over whichever models you choose: one container, a managed
Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS URL. Your conversations stay in your own database, in the EU.

## What this deploys

- **Open WebUI** from the official image, on one m1.medium VM, container port 8080.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so users and chat history survive every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

It does not include a model. Point it at OpenAI, at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or at an
Ollama you already run.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Open WebUI on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The three that actually break it

**The bundled Ollama.** Open WebUI's own compose ships an `ollama` service next to the app.
Copying it onto a VM with no GPU downloads gigabytes, fills the disk and then runs inference on
the CPU. Deploy the app on its own.

**The database.** Without `DATABASE_URL` the app uses SQLite inside the container, and every
chat vanishes on the next redeploy. It does not warn you.

**The secret key.** Set `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` yourself and keep it. Change it and everyone is
logged out and anything derived from it stops decrypting.

## Claiming the admin account

The first account to sign up becomes the administrator, and that is true from the moment the URL
resolves. Run this as soon as the deploy reports ready.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim the Open WebUI admin account, and PROVE it took.
#   ./claim-admin.sh openwebui-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud you@example.com
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"
EMAIL="${2:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host> <email>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
PASS="[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Body on stdin, never in argv: an argument would show up in ps for every user on the machine.
post() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "https://$HOST$1" \
           -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-; }

code=$(printf '{"name":"Admin","email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" \
  | post /api/v1/auths/signup)
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "signup failed: HTTP $code" >&2
  echo "if this says the instance already has users, someone else claimed it. Delete and redeploy." >&2
  cat "$TMP/body" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# A 200 on signup does NOT prove the account can sign in again. This is the actual proof.
code=$(printf '{"email":"%s","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$EMAIL" "$PASS" | post /api/v1/auths/signin)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the account exists but it does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# The first account is meant to be the administrator. Confirm it, do not assume it.
grep -q '"role":"admin"' "$TMP/body" \
  || { echo "signed in, but this account is not an admin. Someone claimed it first." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account claimed, and the sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Email:    $EMAIL
  Password: [REDACTED:value]

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
Next: turn signups off in the admin panel if this is meant to be private.
EOF
```

# Open WebUI on redu — full deployment report

**Date:** 2026-08-16
**Operator:** Claude Code (Opus 5), driving the redu MCP
**redu account:** «REDACTED:env:013044ef»
**Deployment id:** 420 — **provisioned, verified, then destroyed the same session**
**Working directory:** `/home/milos/Desktop/tests_lib/open-webui`

---

## 1. Executive summary

Deployed Open WebUI to redu.cloud from a single-service compose file authored locally, wired to a
managed Postgres on its own private VM, behind a TLS-terminated `*.redu.cloud` hostname. Claimed
the admin account, verified the deploy functionally (not just "the probe went green"), folded the
lessons back into `redu.md`, then tore the app VM down at the user's request.

**Outcome: success, no failed builds, no retries.** Measured cost matched the pre-deploy estimate
to the penny (GBP 0.0452/hr). Total wall clock from `deploy_compose` to `ready`: **~10 minutes**.

The starting point was a directory containing exactly one file — `redu.md` — a runbook carrying a
plan, 15 hard-won quirks, and an admin-claim script. Everything else in this report was produced
during the session.

---

## 2. Final deployed state (before teardown)

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| URL | `https://openwebui-qz3t1fo9.redu.cloud` (TLS, cert verified) |
| App VM | `openwebui` — `0cc2fe0f-14d5-4819-a8b6-1d9e89306f01` |
| Flavor | m1.medium — 2 vCPU / 4096 MB |
| Private IP | [ip] |
| Container | `app-src-open-webui-1`, image `ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:v0.11.0` |
| Port | 8080 host → 8080 container |
| Managed Postgres | db #123 `openwebui`, VM `db-openwebui`, m1.small, PG 16, private IP [ip]:5432 |
| Persistence | named volume `app-src_open-webui-data` → `/app/backend/data` |
| Private network | `f7102e8d-9800-48d7-80a9-8369091d7cad` |
| SSH keypair | `redu-deploy-test` |
| Source mode | upload (tarball), not git |

### Cost

| Resource | Rate | Monthly (730h) |
|---|---|---|
| App VM m1.medium | GBP 0.0278/hr | GBP 20.29 |
| Managed Postgres m1.small | GBP 0.0174/hr | GBP 12.70 |
| **Total** | **GBP 0.0452/hr** | **GBP 32.99** |

The `redu.md` frontmatter predicted `hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452`. The measured figure was identical.

---

## 3. What was actually run, in order

1. **Read `redu.md`.** The runbook is the spec: it dictated compose-not-app, upload-not-git,
   port 8080, managed Postgres, one service, and the admin-claim procedure.
2. **`whoami`** — verified the credential with a real round-trip. Quota: 9 instances, 16 vCPU,
   34 GB RAM available.
3. **`check_deploy_prerequisites`** — auto-selected network `f7102e8d…` and keypair
   `redu-deploy-test`. Mode: guided.
4. **Resolved the image tag.** Queried the GitHub releases API for the latest release
   (`v0.11.0`, published 2026-07-27), then confirmed the tag actually exists on ghcr by minting an
   anonymous pull token and requesting the manifest — `HTTP 200` for both `v0.11.0` and `0.11.0`.
   Pinning a tag you have not confirmed exists is how a deploy fails at pull time.
5. **Wrote `docker-compose.yml`** — one service, no `ollama`, named volume, all secrets by
   reference only.
6. **`plan_deploy`** — passed `redu.md` and the compose file verbatim for server-side parsing.
   Returned the cost, a quota feasibility verdict, and 5 preflight items (§6).
7. **Wrote `redu-deploy-plan.md`** — mandatory pre-deploy artifact.
8. **Asked the user** for the one genuine decision (VM size), the model provider, and drive mode.
   Answers: m1.medium, no provider, YOLO for the remainder.
9. **`prepare_upload`** → ran the returned tar+curl block → `source_token`.
   Verified the response's `size_bytes` (6715) equalled the local tarball's byte size — proof the
   uploaded artifact was the one just built, not a stale file.
10. **`deploy_compose`** — flavor_id `3`, `database: managed`, `db_engine: postgres`,
    `db_flavor_id: 2`, port 8080, pre-generated `dname`, env carrying the secret key and app URL.
11. **Polled to ready** — watched phases `installing` → `building` (1.25 GB image pull) → `done`.
12. **Claimed the admin account** the moment `/health` returned 200.
13. **Verified the deploy over SSH and HTTP** (§5).
14. **`get_deployment` with `redu_md`** — server-side merge, then wrote both files back and added
    7 new quirks the merge does not write itself.
15. **`delete_deployment(420)`** — teardown (§9).

---

## 4. Decisions made, and why

### Pinned `v0.11.0` instead of `:main`
`redu.md` asks for a release tag once you know which one you ran. Rather than deploy `:main` and
backfill the tag afterwards, the release was resolved *before* deploying and the tag verified
against the registry — so the file records a pin that was actually exercised.

### One service. The `ollama` service was never written.
Upstream's compose bundles `ollama/ollama` beside the app. On a GPU-less 4 GB VM that pulls
gigabytes of image plus gigabytes of weights, fills the disk, then runs inference on CPU.
The compose here has exactly one service; the model provider is reached over the network.

### m1.medium, overriding `plan_deploy`
`plan_deploy` sized the app at **m1.large** (GBP 0.066/hr) once `needs_compose: true` was declared.
`redu.md` recorded **m1.medium**. redu surfaced the disagreement rather than silently resolving it,
which was correct — the recorded value is intent, and the reason behind it is real: the RAG
pipeline loads a sentence-transformers embedding model into the app process on first use, so
chat-only and document-embedding have very different memory profiles. This was put to the user
as the one decision worth their attention. They chose m1.medium, saving GBP 0.021/hr (~32%).

### Pre-generated the hostname
The preflight flagged this app as one that is told its own URL. A bare label gets a random 8-char
suffix appended by redu, so anything wired to the bare name breaks. The full form
`openwebui-qz3t1fo9.redu.cloud` was generated locally, passed as `dname`, and `WEBUI_URL` was set
to that same string — so the app's self-URL is correct and stable across redeploys.

### No `migrate_command`
Open WebUI runs its own migrations on container start. The classic redu failure — deploy passes
the probe, then 502s because the schema was never created — does not apply here. Verified by the
app serving real authenticated API calls immediately.

### `ENABLE_OLLAMA_API=false`
With no Ollama deployed, the default would leave the app probing `localhost:11434` — nothing on
this VM — and paying a timeout on every model-list load for a service deliberately not deployed.

### Secrets by reference only
`WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` (48 random alphanumerics), `WEBUI_URL` and `DATABASE_URL` are `${VAR}`
references in the compose and real values only in deploy-time env. A post-hoc scan of every file
in the working directory confirmed neither the secret key nor the admin password appears on disk.

---

## 5. Verification — what was proven, and how

`status: ready` means one health probe passed. It does not mean the app is correctly wired. Each
claim below was checked against the running system.

| Claim | Method | Result |
|---|---|---|
| App serves publicly | `GET /` | 200 |
| TLS valid | curl `ssl_verify_result` | 0 (verified) |
| App is healthy | `GET /health` | 200 at ~590s after deploy start |
| Right image running | `docker ps` on the VM | `ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:v0.11.0` |
| Exactly one service | `docker ps` | 1 container, no `ollama` |
| Bound to all interfaces | `docker ps` ports | `0.0.0.0:8080->8080/tcp` |
| Restarts on boot | compose `restart: unless-stopped` | present |
| **Really on Postgres** | `printenv DATABASE_URL` in container | `postgresql://appuser@[ip]:5432/app` |
| **Not on SQLite** | `ls /app/backend/data/webui.db` | No such file — the fallback never engaged |
| Secret key set | length of `$WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` | 48 |
| Self-URL correct | `printenv WEBUI_URL` | `https://openwebui-qz3t1fo9.redu.cloud` |
| Ollama probing off | `printenv ENABLE_OLLAMA_API` | `false` |
| Data on a volume | `docker inspect` mounts | `volume app-src_open-webui-data → /app/backend/data` |
| Admin account works | POST `/api/v1/auths/signin` | 200, `"role":"admin"` |
| Model list | `GET /api/models` with admin token | `{"data":[]}` — expected, no provider |

The database check is the one that matters most. Open WebUI's SQLite fallback is **silent**: with
no `DATABASE_URL` it writes to `sqlite:///{DATA_DIR}/webui.db` inside the container, comes up
perfectly healthy, and loses every chat, user and setting at the next redeploy with no error.
A green health check cannot distinguish the two configurations. The absence of `webui.db`, paired
with a `DATABASE_URL` pointing at the managed instance and a signup that succeeded, is what proves
the write path reached Postgres.

Similarly, the admin claim was not trusted on its `200`. A successful signup does not prove the
account can sign in again, so the script re-authenticates and asserts `"role":"admin"` — catching
both a broken account and the case where someone else claimed the instance first.

---

## 6. Preflight items from `plan_deploy`, and their disposition

`plan_deploy` returned 5 known failure patterns, each learned from a real failed build.

| Preflight | Disposition |
|---|---|
| Bind `0.0.0.0`, not loopback | Satisfied by the official image; confirmed `0.0.0.0:8080->8080/tcp` |
| Must start on every boot, never a first-boot-only script | `restart: unless-stopped` in the compose |
| App is told its own URL — generate `dname` up front | Done: `dname` pre-generated, `WEBUI_URL` wired to the identical string |
| Schema on first boot, else pass `migrate_command` | Not needed — Open WebUI self-migrates; verified by live authenticated API use |
| Recorded flavor (m1.medium) differs from planned (m1.large) | Escalated to the user as a real decision; m1.medium chosen and passed explicitly |

---

## 7. Problems encountered

**None blocked the deploy.** Three things were discovered that the runbook did not know:

1. **The VM runs Docker, not Podman.** The `deploy_compose` tool documentation describes
   podman-compose, and the first verification attempt failed with `sudo: podman: command not
   found`. The engine is `docker`, and the container is named after the upload directory
   (`app-src-open-webui-1`), not the compose service name. Recovered by probing for available
   binaries. Recorded as a quirk.

2. **`plan_deploy` now sizes this app at m1.large.** The runbook's m1.medium is not what the
   planner picks once `needs_compose: true` is declared. Left unnoticed this silently costs 46%
   more per hour. Recorded as a quirk with the instruction to pass `flavor_id` explicitly.

3. **`redu.md`'s YAML frontmatter did not parse.** A quirk string contained `\"\${DATABASE_URL}\"`
   — and `\$` is not a valid escape inside a double-quoted YAML scalar, so a strict parser
   (PyYAML) raised `found unknown escape character '$'`. This was **pre-existing** in the original
   file, not introduced here, and redu's own server-side parser tolerated it — the memory digest
   came back correctly populated. Fixed to `\"${DATABASE_URL}\"` and the whole frontmatter
   re-validated: parses clean, 22 quirks, all keys intact.

---

## 8. Files produced

All paths under `/home/milos/Desktop/tests_lib/open-webui/`.

| File | Status | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `redu.md` | **modified** | The runbook. Server-side merged via `get_deployment`, plus 7 new quirks, the compose file inlined, a post-deploy verification section, the real deploy-log entry, and the YAML escape fix. 15 → 22 quirks. |
| `docker-compose.yml` | **new** | The one-service stack that was deployed. The artifact `prepare_upload` tarred. |
| `claim-admin.sh` | **new** | Admin-claim script from the runbook, made executable and actually run. |
| `redu-deploy-plan.md` | **new** | Pre-deploy estimate, then overwritten with `get_deployment`'s real provisioned values plus a verification table. |
| `DEPLOYMENT-REPORT.md` | **new** | This report. |

### Quirks added to `redu.md` for the next operator

1. Measured timings — ~10 min to ready, `/health` 200 at ~590s; ten minutes of silence is not a failure.
2. The VM runs **docker**, not podman; container is `app-src-open-webui-1`.
3. How to *prove* the Postgres wiring rather than assume it (the two commands).
4. `plan_deploy` sizes this at m1.large — pass `flavor_id: "3"` explicitly.
5. Generate the `dname` up front and wire `WEBUI_URL` to that exact value.
6. No `migrate_command` needed — the app self-migrates.
7. Set `ENABLE_OLLAMA_API=false` when there is no Ollama to point at.

---

## 9. Teardown

At the user's request, `delete_deployment(420)` was run after verification.

| Resource | State |
|---|---|
| Deployment 420 | **deleted** — absent from `list_deployments` |
| App VM `0cc2fe0f-…` | **destroyed** with the deployment |
| `https://openwebui-qz3t1fo9.redu.cloud` | **dead** — no response, DNS/proxy host removed |
| Named volume `app-src_open-webui-data` | destroyed with the VM |
| **Managed Postgres db #123** | ⚠️ **STILL RUNNING AND BILLING at GBP 0.0174/hr (~GBP 12.70/mo)** |

`delete_deployment` never deletes the managed database — that is deliberate data-safety behaviour,
so chat history is not lost by accident. **To stop billing entirely, `delete_database(123)` must be
run separately.** That call is irreversible, so it was not made without explicit instruction.

Two unrelated deployments on the account — `langflow` (#421) and `umami` (#419), with their
databases #124 and #122 — were left untouched.

### Credentials

The admin account and `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` were generated during the session, handed to the user in
chat, and deliberately never written to any file — `redu.md` is a committed artifact read by the
next operator. Both are now defunct: the app VM and its data volume are destroyed. A scan of the
working directory confirms neither value appears on disk.

---

## 10. Verdict

The runbook worked. Every quirk it warned about was real, the cost estimate was exact, and the
three documented ways this app breaks — the bundled Ollama, the silent SQLite fallback, and the
secret key — were each avoided by design rather than discovered by failure. The deploy needed one
genuine human decision (VM size), and the runbook had already framed why it mattered.

What the next operator gets that this one did not: the true container engine, the real timings, a
two-command proof that the database is wired, and a warning that the planner will now quietly
upsize the VM unless told otherwise.

2. **`whoami`** — verified the credential with a real round-trip. Quota: 9 instances, 16 vCPU,
   34 GB RAM available.
3. **`check_deploy_prerequisites`** — auto-selected network `f7102e8d…` and keypair
   `redu-deploy-test`. Mode: guided.
4. **Resolved the image tag.** Queried the GitHub releases API for the latest release
   (`v0.11.0`, published 2026-07-27), then confirmed the tag actually exists on ghcr by minting an
   anonymous pull token and requesting the manifest — `HTTP 200` for both `v0.11.0` and `0.11.0`.
   Pinning a tag you have not confirmed exists is how a deploy fails at pull time.
5. **Wrote `docker-compose.yml`** — one service, no `ollama`, named volume, all secrets by
   reference only.
6. **`plan_deploy`** — passed `redu.md` and the compose file verbatim for server-side parsing.
   Returned the cost, a quota feasibility verdict, and 5 preflight items (§6).
7. **Wrote `redu-deploy-plan.md`** — mandatory pre-deploy artifact.
8. **Asked the user** for the one genuine decision (VM size), the model provider, and drive mode.
   Answers: m1.medium, no provider, YOLO for the remainder.
9. **`prepare_upload`** → ran the returned tar+curl block → `source_token`.
   Verified the response's `size_bytes` (6715) equalled the local tarball's byte size — proof the
   uploaded artifact was the one just built, not a stale file.
10. **`deploy_compose`** — flavor_id `3`, `database: managed`, `db_engine: postgres`,
    `db_flavor_id: 2`, port 8080, pre-generated `dname`, env carrying the secret key and app URL.
11. **Polled to ready** — watched phases `installing` → `building` (1.25 GB image pull) → `done`.
12. **Claimed the admin account** the moment `/health` returned 200.
13. **Verified the deploy over SSH and HTTP** (§5).
14. **`get_deployment` with `redu_md`** — server-side merge, then wrote both files back and added
    7 new quirks the merge does not write itself.
15. **`delete_deployment(420)`** — teardown (§9).

---

## 4. Decisions made, and why

### Pinned `v0.11.0` instead of `:main`
`redu.md` asks for a release tag once you know which one you ran. Rather than deploy `:main` and
backfill the tag afterwards, the release was resolved *before* deploying and the tag verified
against the registry — so the file records a pin that was actually exercised.

### One service. The `ollama` service was never written.
Upstream's compose bundles `ollama/ollama` beside the app. On a GPU-less 4 GB VM that pulls
gigabytes of image plus gigabytes of weights, fills the disk, then runs inference on CPU.
The compose here has exactly one service; the model provider is reached over the network.

### m1.medium, overriding `plan_deploy`
`plan_deploy` sized the app at **m1.large** (GBP 0.066/hr) once `needs_compose: true` was declared.
`redu.md` recorded **m1.medium**. redu surfaced the disagreement rather than silently resolving it,
which was correct — the recorded value is intent, and the reason behind it is real: the RAG
pipeline loads a sentence-transformers embedding model into the app process on first use, so
chat-only and document-embedding have very different memory profiles. This was put to the user
as the one decision worth their attention. They chose m1.medium, saving GBP 0.021/hr (~32%).

### Pre-generated the hostname
The preflight flagged this app as one that is told its own URL. A bare label gets a random 8-char
suffix appended by redu, so anything wired to the bare name breaks. The full form
`openwebui-qz3t1fo9.redu.cloud` was generated locally, passed as `dname`, and `WEBUI_URL` was set
to that same string — so the app's self-URL is correct and stable across redeploys.

### No `migrate_command`
Open WebUI runs its own migrations on container start. The classic redu failure — deploy passes
the probe, then 502s because the schema was never created — does not apply here. Verified by the
app serving real authenticated API calls immediately.

### `ENABLE_OLLAMA_API=false`
With no Ollama deployed, the default would leave the app probing `localhost:11434` — nothing on
this VM — and paying a timeout on every model-list load for a service deliberately not deployed.

### Secrets by reference only
`WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` (48 random alphanumerics), `WEBUI_URL` and `DATABASE_URL` are `${VAR}`
references in the compose and real values only in deploy-time env. A post-hoc scan of every file
in the working directory confirmed neither the secret key nor the admin password appears on disk.

---

## 5. Verification — what was proven, and how

`status: ready` means one health probe passed. It does not mean the app is correctly wired. Each
claim below was checked against the running system.

| Claim | Method | Result |
|---|---|---|
| App serves publicly | `GET /` | 200 |
| TLS valid | curl `ssl_verify_result` | 0 (verified) |
| App is healthy | `GET /health` | 200 at ~590s after deploy start |
| Right image running | `docker ps` on the VM | `ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:v0.11.0` |
| Exactly one service | `docker ps` | 1 container, no `ollama` |
| Bound to all interfaces | `docker ps` ports | `0.0.0.0:8080->8080/tcp` |
| Restarts on boot | compose `restart: unless-stopped` | present |
| **Really on Postgres** | `printenv DATABASE_URL` in container | `postgresql://appuser@[ip]:5432/app` |
| **Not on SQLite** | `ls /app/backend/data/webui.db` | No such file — the fallback never engaged |
| Secret key set | length of `$WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` | 48 |
| Self-URL correct | `printenv WEBUI_URL` | `https://openwebui-qz3t1fo9.redu.cloud` |
| Ollama probing off | `printenv ENABLE_OLLAMA_API` | `false` |
| Data on a volume | `docker inspect` mounts | `volume app-src_open-webui-data → /app/backend/data` |
| Admin account works | POST `/api/v1/auths/signin` | 200, `"role":"admin"` |
| Model list | `GET /api/models` with admin token | `{"data":[]}` — expected, no provider |

The database check is the one that matters most. Open WebUI's SQLite fallback is **silent**: with
no `DATABASE_URL` it writes to `sqlite:///{DATA_DIR}/webui.db` inside the container, comes up
perfectly healthy, and loses every chat, user and setting at the next redeploy with no error.
A green health check cannot distinguish the two configurations. The absence of `webui.db`, paired
with a `DATABASE_URL` pointing at the managed instance and a signup that succeeded, is what proves
the write path reached Postgres.

Similarly, the admin claim was not trusted on its `200`. A successful signup does not prove the
account can sign in again, so the script re-authenticates and asserts `"role":"admin"` — catching
both a broken account and the case where someone else claimed the instance first.

---

## 6. Preflight items from `plan_deploy`, and their disposition

`plan_deploy` returned 5 known failure patterns, each learned from a real failed build.

| Preflight | Disposition |
|---|---|
| Bind `0.0.0.0`, not loopback | Satisfied by the official image; confirmed `0.0.0.0:8080->8080/tcp` |
| Must start on every boot, never a first-boot-only script | `restart: unless-stopped` in the compose |
| App is told its own URL — generate `dname` up front | Done: `dname` pre-generated, `WEBUI_URL` wired to the identical string |
| Schema on first boot, else pass `migrate_command` | Not needed — Open WebUI self-migrates; verified by live authenticated API use |
| Recorded flavor (m1.medium) differs from planned (m1.large) | Escalated to the user as a real decision; m1.medium chosen and passed explicitly |

---

## 7. Problems encountered

**None blocked the deploy.** Three things were discovered that the runbook did not know:

1. **The VM runs Docker, not Podman.** The `deploy_compose` tool documentation describes
   podman-compose, and the first verification attempt failed with `sudo: podman: command not
   found`. The engine is `docker`, and the container is named after the upload directory
   (`app-src-open-webui-1`), not the compose service name. Recovered by probing for available
   binaries. Recorded as a quirk.

2. **`plan_deploy` now sizes this app at m1.large.** The runbook's m1.medium is not what the
   planner picks once `needs_compose: true` is declared. Left unnoticed this silently costs 46%
   more per hour. Recorded as a quirk with the instruction to pass `flavor_id` explicitly.

3. **`redu.md`'s YAML frontmatter did not parse.** A quirk string contained `\"\${DATABASE_URL}\"`
   — and `\$` is not a valid escape inside a double-quoted YAML scalar, so a strict parser
   (PyYAML) raised `found unknown escape character '$'`. This was **pre-existing** in the original
   file, not introduced here, and redu's own server-side parser tolerated it — the memory digest
   came back correctly populated. Fixed to `\"${DATABASE_URL}\"` and the whole frontmatter
   re-validated: parses clean, 22 quirks, all keys intact.

---

## 8. Files produced

All paths under `/home/milos/Desktop/tests_lib/open-webui/`.

| File | Status | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `redu.md` | **modified** | The runbook. Server-side merged via `get_deployment`, plus 7 new quirks, the compose file inlined, a post-deploy verification section, the real deploy-log entry, and the YAML escape fix. 15 → 22 quirks. |
| `docker-compose.yml` | **new** | The one-service stack that was deployed. The artifact `prepare_upload` tarred. |
| `claim-admin.sh` | **new** | Admin-claim script from the runbook, made executable and actually run. |
| `redu-deploy-plan.md` | **new** | Pre-deploy estimate, then overwritten with `get_deployment`'s real provisioned values plus a verification table. |
| `DEPLOYMENT-REPORT.md` | **new** | This report. |

### Quirks added to `redu.md` for the next operator

1. Measured timings — ~10 min to ready, `/health` 200 at ~590s; ten minutes of silence is not a failure.
2. The VM runs **docker**, not podman; container is `app-src-open-webui-1`.
3. How to *prove* the Postgres wiring rather than assume it (the two commands).
4. `plan_deploy` sizes this at m1.large — pass `flavor_id: "3"` explicitly.
5. Generate the `dname` up front and wire `WEBUI_URL` to that exact value.
6. No `migrate_command` needed — the app self-migrates.
7. Set `ENABLE_OLLAMA_API=false` when there is no Ollama to point at.

---

## 9. Teardown

At the user's request, `delete_deployment(420)` was run after verification.

| Resource | State |
|---|---|
| Deployment 420 | **deleted** — absent from `list_deployments` |
| App VM `0cc2fe0f-…` | **destroyed** with the deployment |
| `https://openwebui-qz3t1fo9.redu.cloud` | **dead** — no response, DNS/proxy host removed |
| Named volume `app-src_open-webui-data` | destroyed with the VM |
| **Managed Postgres db #123** | ⚠️ **STILL RUNNING AND BILLING at GBP 0.0174/hr (~GBP 12.70/mo)** |

`delete_deployment` never deletes the managed database — that is deliberate data-safety behaviour,
so chat history is not lost by accident. **To stop billing entirely, `delete_database(123)` must be
run separately.** That call is irreversible, so it was not made without explicit instruction.

Two unrelated deployments on the account — `langflow` (#421) and `umami` (#419), with their
databases #124 and #122 — were left untouched.

### Credentials

The admin account and `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` were generated during the session, handed to the user in
chat, and deliberately never written to any file — `redu.md` is a committed artifact read by the
next operator. Both are now defunct: the app VM and its data volume are destroyed. A scan of the
working directory confirms neither value appears on disk.

---

## 10. Verdict

The runbook worked. Every quirk it warned about was real, the cost estimate was exact, and the
three documented ways this app breaks — the bundled Ollama, the silent SQLite fallback, and the
secret key — were each avoided by design rather than discovered by failure. The deploy needed one
genuine human decision (VM size), and the runbook had already framed why it mattered.

What the next operator gets that this one did not: the true container engine, the real timings, a
two-command proof that the database is wired, and a warning that the planner will now quietly
upsize the VM unless told otherwise.
